medical.title: How cells respond differently to a cancer-causing gene
medical.summary: Researchers at NYU Abu Dhabi have discovered that a single cancer-causing gene can trigger different responses in cells, with some helping to prevent tumors while others may contribute to their development.

medical.title: Early interventions for depression tied to better cancer survival
medical.summary: Depression may be an overlooked factor in cancer outcomes, according to a large SEER-Medicare analysis of more than 265,000 adults with six common cancers. Researchers found that patients with major depressive disorder had a higher risk of dying from their cancer, while those who received psychotherapy within four weeks of their cancer diagnosis had a 21% lower risk of cancer-specific mortality. Only 3% of patients with depression received psychotherapy in that early window, however.

medical.title: Patented polymer shows promising results for the oral drug delivery industry
medical.summary: The most common way to take medicine is orally, which requires the drug to dissolve and absorb into the systemic circulation. Oral drugs are often formulated with a range of traditional excipients, but a new polymer made from renewable raw materials and patented by Åbo Akademi University (Finland) offers a promising alternative. This is the conclusion of Vishal Kumar's doctoral dissertation.

medical.title: Ready, set, exhale: Breathing out linked to faster responses
medical.summary: Imagine swimmers on starting blocks, poised to dive at the sound of the starting horn, or a driver traveling at 60 mph (97 kilometers per hour) who suddenly needs to brake to avoid a collision. A fraction of a second in response time could mean the difference between winning and losing—or between life and death.

medical.title: Short-course radiation therapy better preserves physical function before pancreatic cancer surgery
medical.summary: Patients preparing for pancreatic cancer surgery maintained better physical function and experienced less fatigue with five treatments of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) than with 28 treatments of conventional radiation therapy given with chemotherapy, according to a randomized Phase II clinical trial.

medical.title: Fractionated radiosurgery reduces cancer recurrence after surgery for large brain metastases, trial finds
medical.summary: Delivering focused radiation therapy over three to five sessions after surgery for a large brain metastasis reduced the risk of cancer returning at the surgical site compared with delivering the radiation in a single session, according to results of the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology A071801 presented today at the plenary session of the American Society for Radiation Oncology in Boston.

medical.title: Radiosurgery linked to longer survival for small cell lung cancer with brain metastases
medical.summary: Patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC) that had spread to the brain lived a median of 17 months after focused stereotactic radiosurgery, compared with nine months after an advanced form of whole-brain radiation therapy, an unexpected secondary finding from the first randomized Phase III trial to compare the treatment approaches in this population.

medical.title: Five-treatment radiation therapy offers an effective nonsurgical alternative for localized prostate cancer
medical.summary: Five-treatment stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) provided excellent long-term cancer control with fewer urinary and sexual side effects than surgery in the first randomized trial to directly compare the treatments for localized prostate cancer.

medical.title: Frequent cannabis use tied to more severe epilepsy
medical.summary: Adults with hard-to-treat epilepsy who used cannabis most days had more than twice as many convulsive seizures per year and became resistant to antiseizure medications more quickly than nonusers, according to new research from Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.

medical.title: AI and fruit fly tests link BRSK1 gene to rare neurodevelopmental disorder
medical.summary: Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine, the Duncan Neurological Research Institute (Duncan NRI) at Texas Children's Hospital, the Texome Project and collaborating institutions have identified variants in the BRSK1 gene as a likely diagnosis for individuals with a rare and complex neurodevelopmental disorder who had not received an explanation for their condition.

medical.title: Fractionated radiosurgery reduces cancer recurrence after surgery for large brain metastases
medical.summary: Delivering focused radiation therapy over three to five sessions after surgery for a large brain metastasis reduced the risk of cancer returning at the surgical site compared with delivering the radiation in a single session, according to the first randomized Phase III clinical trial directly comparing the approaches.

medical.title: Incisionless radiosurgery shows promise for severe, treatment-resistant depression
medical.summary: A highly focused, incisionless form of radiation therapy significantly reduced symptoms of major depression and thoughts of suicide among patients with severe, treatment-resistant psychiatric illness in a prospective observational study. Results were presented at the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) Annual Meeting.

medical.title: New AI tool can predict where glioblastoma is most likely to return after initial surgery
medical.summary: A new AI-based model can predict where glioblastoma is most likely to return after initial surgery, potentially giving doctors a chance to treat it before it becomes visible on MRI.

medical.title: New method automatically maps myelin patterns in the brain, revealing signs of injury
medical.summary: Myelin, the insulating sheath around nerve fibers, is essential for fast, healthy signaling in the brain. Its patterns vary widely across brain regions. Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have developed a computer method that can quantify these patterns automatically, without manually labeling tissue images. The findings are published in Brain Structure and Function.

medical.title: 165,000+ pounds of pork, beef and goat recalled over USDA inspection mark
medical.summary: A North Carolina company is recalling 167,639 pounds (76,000 kilograms) of raw goat, beef and pork that never went through required federal inspection, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials announced.

medical.title: Diabetes study finds keeping blood sugar too steady may come at a price
medical.summary: People with diabetes reported better quality of life after days when their glucose stayed largely within a healthy range, even when levels fluctuated more than usual. The unexpected finding suggests that pursuing extremely tight glucose control may sometimes come with a hidden lifestyle burden.

medical.title: Brain stimulation could reshape how you learn new skills
medical.summary: Whether learning a new piano piece or adapting your tennis serve, acquiring physical skills depends on your brain's ability to strengthen and refine neural connections. Researchers are exploring whether technology can accelerate this process.

medical.title: Pre-exercise caffeine enhances repeated sprint performance for at least 3.5 hours
medical.summary: Caffeine is one of the most widely used performance-enhancing supplements in sports. Despite its established benefits, how long they persist and how physiological responses change over that period remain unclear.

medical.title: People fitted with synthetic owl ears learn to localize sound (a little) better
medical.summary: People are very good at pinpointing the source of a sound, but not as good as barn owls. With their ears, barn owls can pinpoint the source of a sound with exceptional accuracy, which comes in handy when they hunt for prey at night. Their asymmetrical ears are a unique adaptation in the animal kingdom.

medical.title: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
medical.summary: A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. Decaf was associated with better learning and memory, while caffeinated coffee appeared to reduce anxiety and improve attention.

medical.title: More than meets the ear: What music practice means for a developing brain
medical.summary: Sitting through an 8-year-old's shaky rendition of Christian Petzold's "Minuet in G" may be music to a proud parent's ear. To everyone else at the recital, it might not sound like encore material. Behind those wobbly notes, however, a far more complex mental production is underway—and the skills it exercises may reach far beyond music.

medical.title: How missing pieces of the Y chromosome drive cancer in men
medical.summary: A new study found that cancer cells selectively chip away gene-rich sections of the Y chromosome, triggering changes that regulate tumor growth. Co-led by University of Arizona Cancer Center physician-scientist Dr. Dan Theodorescu, the paper, "Recurrent deletions and regulatory disruption of the Y chromosome in cancer," was published in the journal Communications Biology.

medical.title: Genetic profiling could help tailor hormone therapy for prostate cancer after surgery
medical.summary: A recent analysis of the NRG-RTOG 0534 "SPPORT" clinical trial evaluated the Luminal B (LumB) molecular subtype using the PAM50 genomic classifier to determine whether tumor biology could help identify patients most likely to benefit from hormone therapy.

medical.title: Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
medical.summary: Spaceflight may dramatically change the gut within weeks, causing bacteria to break down more protein as food moves more slowly through the intestines. The shift could help explain astronaut constipation and may have wider effects on health, making it an important concern for future missions to Mars.

medical.title: Turning to AI for health answers may signal anxiety, depression among young adults
medical.summary: Young adults who use generative artificial intelligence to ask health-related questions are more likely to screen positive for clinically significant anxiety and depression than those who do not use AI for health issues, according to a new study led by University of Florida researcher Yusen Zhai.

science.title: Organic chemists harness AI to uncover how fast chemical reactions proceed
science.summary: Chemists routinely optimize reactions to maximize the yield of their desired products, but understanding why those reactions work can require laborious experiments that track reactions over time. Researchers at the University of Tokyo have developed a method to extract hidden information about reaction speeds from yield data obtained during reaction optimization, using machine learning and rate equations developed by chemists.

science.title: Generous paternal leave policies improve maternal and newborn health, family finances and workplace equality
science.summary: When our second child was born, my spouse had several weeks of paternity leave under his parental leave policy at work.

science.title: The joy of song: Where songbirds came from and why we should listen to them
science.summary: In 2001, I had an epiphany while making my first trip to Australia. Walking across a remote sheep station in the dusty west, my ears were suddenly filled with the rich, spirited song of three pied butcherbirds.

science.title: Halting plastic flows into oceans by 2050 may not stop microplastic buildup
science.summary: Halting new marine plastic inputs by 2050 is the core objective of the Osaka Blue Ocean Vision, which was shared and endorsed alongside the G20 Implementation Framework for Actions on Marine Plastic Litter. However, stopping new plastic inputs will not remove existing marine debris, which can gradually fragment into microplastics that are difficult and costly to remove. Source reduction must therefore be accompanied by cleanup of legacy plastic debris.

science.title: Bullfrog brains can make their own backup fuel
science.summary: For decades, scientists believed most animals relied on a steady supply of glucose, the body's primary fuel source, to power their brains. When glucose runs out, neural activity begins to fail, potentially leading to lasting brain damage.

science.title: What's behind part-time work for men
science.summary: In Switzerland, 40% of the working population works part-time, according to 2025 figures from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO). Women account for the lion's share: 60% of women in the workforce are employed part-time, while only more than 1 in 5 men work part-time. These figures place Switzerland second among the 38 countries of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in terms of part-time work, just behind the Netherlands.

science.title: NASA ORBIT Challenge 2027
science.summary: The NASA ORBIT (Opportunities in Research, Business, Innovation, and Technology for the Workforce) Challenge invites university and community college students nationwide to work with real NASA intellectual property and mission challenges. Choose your path: develop commercial applications of NASA patents that solve problems here on Earth (ORBIT Earth), or design next-generation technologies for space exploration […]

science.title: The right timing of treatment keeps resistant cells in check, yeast experiments suggest
science.summary: The development of treatment resistance is one of the key challenges in modern cancer and antibiotic therapy. New therapeutic approaches aim to curb the spread of resistance through the targeted timing of treatment cycles.

science.title: Worm experiments reveal how epigenetic effects persist across generations
science.summary: Every cell in an organism contains the same DNA, which carries all the instructions needed for it to function. Yet cells do not all use the same genes: A nerve cell, for example, does not activate the same genes as a muscle cell. Epigenetics refers to the mechanisms that allow gene activity to be modulated without changing the DNA sequence.

science.title: One of Canada's worst invasive species may have arrived naturally
science.summary: Most invasive species are introduced into the areas where they become damaging. That's part of why they tend to be so successful in taking over new environments and causing billions of dollars in damage.

science.title: What role does high school play in mental health? Feeling connected to other students and staff is key
science.summary: By age 15, an Australian student may have spent as many as 11,000 hours at school.

science.title: Mapping one atom's interaction with light uncovers an unbounded network of quantum states
science.summary: A new graph-theoretic framework provides a unified description of atom-light interactions across regimes ranging from weak to deep-strong coupling.

science.title: 84 cents for every $1: Why indigenous workers earn less in Australia—and what to do about it
science.summary: Indigenous workers in Australia earn 15.9% less per hour on average than all workers—or 84 cents for every $1 earned by non-Indigenous people—our research found.

science.title: Magnetic order survives weak quantum fluctuations in gapless magnets
science.summary: In a new study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers have shown that magnetic order can survive weak quantum fluctuations in disordered magnets that lack an energy gap. The work establishes robust ferromagnetism in the two-dimensional random-bond quantum Ising model, confirming a longstanding conjecture in quantum statistical mechanics.

science.title: Zebrafish reveal wider role for gene linked to human albinism
science.summary: Tiny, striped zebrafish are helping scientists trace how a gene linked to albinism influences eye development, work that may ultimately help explain some of the vision problems experienced by people with the condition and guide the search for new treatments.

science.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Kristie Foster
science.summary: Kristie Foster paved her road to becoming a NASA civil servant with literal miles of dedication. Her work at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, supports NASA’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon, build a Moon Base for an enduring presence on the lunar surface, and ensure American leadership […]

science.title: How routines, rituals and rites of passage are foundations of an inclusive classroom
science.summary: For many families, especially those whose children are disabled or neurodivergent, September is a daunting time. Children often find themselves in a classroom with new faces, spaces or routines.

science.title: How bootmaking in Victorian England helps us think about the future of work
science.summary: Put yourself in the shoes of a bootmaker in 19th-century England. Bootmaking was a sophisticated craft that involved cutting and stitching leather. It required skill, experience and time.

science.title: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
science.summary: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.

science.title: Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending
science.summary: How many times a day do we see messages about protecting our peace, setting boundaries and cutting toxic people out of our lives?

science.title: James Webb reveals why planet formation is a race against time
science.summary: JWST has revealed that young planetary systems lose their planet-building gas through a changing mix of powerful jets, molecular winds, and radiation-driven outflows. As the disks age and their gas disappears, giant planets face a shrinking window to build massive atmospheres.

science.title: Where do nanoparticles go once they enter the body? Scientist helps shape new guidance
science.summary: New international best practice guidance, co-written at ANSTO, sets out how to measure where nanoparticles like titanium dioxide end up in the body and how long they remain. The guidance has been shared by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a forum and knowledge hub for data, analysis and best practices in public policy.

science.title: An ancient human face emerges from pieced together Moroccan fossil remains
science.summary: In the 1960s, a miner working at a mineral extraction site in Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, struck something far more valuable than any mineral in the area: a skull with distinctly humanlike features. After an initial examination, archaeologists excavated further and uncovered more remains, which they estimated to be around 40,000 years old. They identified the main skull as an African Neanderthal and named it Irhoud 1.

science.title: Why higher prices can be a double-edged sword for digital services
science.summary: Paying a steeper price for a subscription service can trigger a familiar impulse: You want to get your money's worth. For companies selling AI tools, cloud computing and other digital services, that can complicate a basic pricing strategy. Raising prices may keep some customers from signing up, but those who do pay may be motivated to use the service more.

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: Organic chemists harness AI to uncover how fast chemical reactions proceed
mix_items.summary: Chemists routinely optimize reactions to maximize the yield of their desired products, but understanding why those reactions work can require laborious experiments that track reactions over time. Researchers at the University of Tokyo have developed a method to extract hidden information about reaction speeds from yield data obtained during reaction optimization, using machine learning and rate equations developed by chemists.

mix_items.summary: Researchers at NYU Abu Dhabi have discovered that a single cancer-causing gene can trigger different responses in cells, with some helping to prevent tumors while others may contribute to their development.

mix_items.title: Early interventions for depression tied to better cancer survival
mix_items.summary: Depression may be an overlooked factor in cancer outcomes, according to a large SEER-Medicare analysis of more than 265,000 adults with six common cancers. Researchers found that patients with major depressive disorder had a higher risk of dying from their cancer, while those who received psychotherapy within four weeks of their cancer diagnosis had a 21% lower risk of cancer-specific mortality. Only 3% of patients with depression received psychotherapy in that early window, however.

mix_items.title: Patented polymer shows promising results for the oral drug delivery industry
mix_items.summary: The most common way to take medicine is orally, which requires the drug to dissolve and absorb into the systemic circulation. Oral drugs are often formulated with a range of traditional excipients, but a new polymer made from renewable raw materials and patented by Åbo Akademi University (Finland) offers a promising alternative. This is the conclusion of Vishal Kumar's doctoral dissertation.

mix_items.title: The joy of song: Where songbirds came from and why we should listen to them
mix_items.summary: In 2001, I had an epiphany while making my first trip to Australia. Walking across a remote sheep station in the dusty west, my ears were suddenly filled with the rich, spirited song of three pied butcherbirds.

mix_items.title: Halting plastic flows into oceans by 2050 may not stop microplastic buildup
mix_items.summary: Halting new marine plastic inputs by 2050 is the core objective of the Osaka Blue Ocean Vision, which was shared and endorsed alongside the G20 Implementation Framework for Actions on Marine Plastic Litter. However, stopping new plastic inputs will not remove existing marine debris, which can gradually fragment into microplastics that are difficult and costly to remove. Source reduction must therefore be accompanied by cleanup of legacy plastic debris.

mix_items.title: Ready, set, exhale: Breathing out linked to faster responses
mix_items.summary: Imagine swimmers on starting blocks, poised to dive at the sound of the starting horn, or a driver traveling at 60 mph (97 kilometers per hour) who suddenly needs to brake to avoid a collision. A fraction of a second in response time could mean the difference between winning and losing—or between life and death.

mix_items.title: Short-course radiation therapy better preserves physical function before pancreatic cancer surgery
mix_items.summary: Patients preparing for pancreatic cancer surgery maintained better physical function and experienced less fatigue with five treatments of stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) than with 28 treatments of conventional radiation therapy given with chemotherapy, according to a randomized Phase II clinical trial.

mix_items.title: Fractionated radiosurgery reduces cancer recurrence after surgery for large brain metastases, trial finds
mix_items.summary: Delivering focused radiation therapy over three to five sessions after surgery for a large brain metastasis reduced the risk of cancer returning at the surgical site compared with delivering the radiation in a single session, according to results of the Alliance for Clinical Trials in Oncology A071801 presented today at the plenary session of the American Society for Radiation Oncology in Boston.

mix_items.title: Bullfrog brains can make their own backup fuel
mix_items.summary: For decades, scientists believed most animals relied on a steady supply of glucose, the body's primary fuel source, to power their brains. When glucose runs out, neural activity begins to fail, potentially leading to lasting brain damage.

mix_items.title: Radiosurgery linked to longer survival for small cell lung cancer with brain metastases
mix_items.summary: Patients with small cell lung cancer (SCLC) that had spread to the brain lived a median of 17 months after focused stereotactic radiosurgery, compared with nine months after an advanced form of whole-brain radiation therapy, an unexpected secondary finding from the first randomized Phase III trial to compare the treatment approaches in this population.

mix_items.title: Five-treatment radiation therapy offers an effective nonsurgical alternative for localized prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: Five-treatment stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) provided excellent long-term cancer control with fewer urinary and sexual side effects than surgery in the first randomized trial to directly compare the treatments for localized prostate cancer.

mix_items.title: What's behind part-time work for men
mix_items.summary: In Switzerland, 40% of the working population works part-time, according to 2025 figures from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO). Women account for the lion's share: 60% of women in the workforce are employed part-time, while only more than 1 in 5 men work part-time. These figures place Switzerland second among the 38 countries of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in terms of part-time work, just behind the Netherlands.

mix_items.title: Frequent cannabis use tied to more severe epilepsy
mix_items.summary: Adults with hard-to-treat epilepsy who used cannabis most days had more than twice as many convulsive seizures per year and became resistant to antiseizure medications more quickly than nonusers, according to new research from Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis.

mix_items.title: AI and fruit fly tests link BRSK1 gene to rare neurodevelopmental disorder
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Baylor College of Medicine, the Duncan Neurological Research Institute (Duncan NRI) at Texas Children's Hospital, the Texome Project and collaborating institutions have identified variants in the BRSK1 gene as a likely diagnosis for individuals with a rare and complex neurodevelopmental disorder who had not received an explanation for their condition.

mix_items.title: Fractionated radiosurgery reduces cancer recurrence after surgery for large brain metastases
mix_items.summary: Delivering focused radiation therapy over three to five sessions after surgery for a large brain metastasis reduced the risk of cancer returning at the surgical site compared with delivering the radiation in a single session, according to the first randomized Phase III clinical trial directly comparing the approaches.

Choose your path: develop commercial applications of NASA patents that solve problems here on Earth (ORBIT Earth), or design next-generation technologies for space exploration […]

mix_items.title: Incisionless radiosurgery shows promise for severe, treatment-resistant depression
mix_items.summary: A highly focused, incisionless form of radiation therapy significantly reduced symptoms of major depression and thoughts of suicide among patients with severe, treatment-resistant psychiatric illness in a prospective observational study. Results were presented at the American Society for Radiation Oncology (ASTRO) Annual Meeting.

mix_items.title: The right timing of treatment keeps resistant cells in check, yeast experiments suggest
mix_items.summary: The development of treatment resistance is one of the key challenges in modern cancer and antibiotic therapy. New therapeutic approaches aim to curb the spread of resistance through the targeted timing of treatment cycles.

mix_items.title: Worm experiments reveal how epigenetic effects persist across generations
mix_items.summary: Every cell in an organism contains the same DNA, which carries all the instructions needed for it to function. Yet cells do not all use the same genes: A nerve cell, for example, does not activate the same genes as a muscle cell. Epigenetics refers to the mechanisms that allow gene activity to be modulated without changing the DNA sequence.

mix_items.title: New AI tool can predict where glioblastoma is most likely to return after initial surgery
mix_items.summary: A new AI-based model can predict where glioblastoma is most likely to return after initial surgery, potentially giving doctors a chance to treat it before it becomes visible on MRI.

mix_items.title: New method automatically maps myelin patterns in the brain, revealing signs of injury
mix_items.summary: Myelin, the insulating sheath around nerve fibers, is essential for fast, healthy signaling in the brain. Its patterns vary widely across brain regions. Researchers at the University of Eastern Finland have developed a computer method that can quantify these patterns automatically, without manually labeling tissue images. The findings are published in Brain Structure and Function.

mix_items.title: 165,000+ pounds of pork, beef and goat recalled over USDA inspection mark
mix_items.summary: A North Carolina company is recalling 167,639 pounds (76,000 kilograms) of raw goat, beef and pork that never went through required federal inspection, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials announced.

mix_items.title: One of Canada's worst invasive species may have arrived naturally
mix_items.summary: Most invasive species are introduced into the areas where they become damaging. That's part of why they tend to be so successful in taking over new environments and causing billions of dollars in damage.

mix_items.title: Diabetes study finds keeping blood sugar too steady may come at a price
mix_items.summary: People with diabetes reported better quality of life after days when their glucose stayed largely within a healthy range, even when levels fluctuated more than usual. The unexpected finding suggests that pursuing extremely tight glucose control may sometimes come with a hidden lifestyle burden.

mix_items.title: What role does high school play in mental health? Feeling connected to other students and staff is key
mix_items.summary: By age 15, an Australian student may have spent as many as 11,000 hours at school.

mix_items.title: Mapping one atom's interaction with light uncovers an unbounded network of quantum states
mix_items.summary: A new graph-theoretic framework provides a unified description of atom-light interactions across regimes ranging from weak to deep-strong coupling.

mix_items.title: Brain stimulation could reshape how you learn new skills
mix_items.summary: Whether learning a new piano piece or adapting your tennis serve, acquiring physical skills depends on your brain's ability to strengthen and refine neural connections. Researchers are exploring whether technology can accelerate this process.

mix_items.title: Pre-exercise caffeine enhances repeated sprint performance for at least 3.5 hours
mix_items.summary: Caffeine is one of the most widely used performance-enhancing supplements in sports. Despite its established benefits, how long they persist and how physiological responses change over that period remain unclear.

mix_items.title: People fitted with synthetic owl ears learn to localize sound (a little) better
mix_items.summary: People are very good at pinpointing the source of a sound, but not as good as barn owls. With their ears, barn owls can pinpoint the source of a sound with exceptional accuracy, which comes in handy when they hunt for prey at night. Their asymmetrical ears are a unique adaptation in the animal kingdom.

mix_items.title: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
mix_items.summary: A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. Decaf was associated with better learning and memory, while caffeinated coffee appeared to reduce anxiety and improve attention.

mix_items.title: More than meets the ear: What music practice means for a developing brain
mix_items.summary: Sitting through an 8-year-old's shaky rendition of Christian Petzold's "Minuet in G" may be music to a proud parent's ear. To everyone else at the recital, it might not sound like encore material. Behind those wobbly notes, however, a far more complex mental production is underway—and the skills it exercises may reach far beyond music.

mix_items.title: 84 cents for every $1: Why indigenous workers earn less in Australia—and what to do about it
mix_items.summary: Indigenous workers in Australia earn 15.9% less per hour on average than all workers—or 84 cents for every $1 earned by non-Indigenous people—our research found.

mix_items.title: Magnetic order survives weak quantum fluctuations in gapless magnets
mix_items.summary: In a new study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers have shown that magnetic order can survive weak quantum fluctuations in disordered magnets that lack an energy gap. The work establishes robust ferromagnetism in the two-dimensional random-bond quantum Ising model, confirming a longstanding conjecture in quantum statistical mechanics.

mix_items.title: Zebrafish reveal wider role for gene linked to human albinism
mix_items.summary: Tiny, striped zebrafish are helping scientists trace how a gene linked to albinism influences eye development, work that may ultimately help explain some of the vision problems experienced by people with the condition and guide the search for new treatments.

mix_items.title: How missing pieces of the Y chromosome drive cancer in men
mix_items.summary: A new study found that cancer cells selectively chip away gene-rich sections of the Y chromosome, triggering changes that regulate tumor growth. Co-led by University of Arizona Cancer Center physician-scientist Dr. Dan Theodorescu, the paper, "Recurrent deletions and regulatory disruption of the Y chromosome in cancer," was published in the journal Communications Biology.

mix_items.title: Genetic profiling could help tailor hormone therapy for prostate cancer after surgery
mix_items.summary: A recent analysis of the NRG-RTOG 0534 "SPPORT" clinical trial evaluated the Luminal B (LumB) molecular subtype using the PAM50 genomic classifier to determine whether tumor biology could help identify patients most likely to benefit from hormone therapy.

mix_items.title: Contractor to Civil Servant: NASA Welcomes Kristie Foster
mix_items.summary: Kristie Foster paved her road to becoming a NASA civil servant with literal miles of dedication. Her work at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, supports NASA’s mission to return American astronauts to the Moon, build a Moon Base for an enduring presence on the lunar surface, and ensure American leadership […]

mix_items.title: Blood tests reveal why astronauts get constipated in space
mix_items.summary: Spaceflight may dramatically change the gut within weeks, causing bacteria to break down more protein as food moves more slowly through the intestines. The shift could help explain astronaut constipation and may have wider effects on health, making it an important concern for future missions to Mars.

mix_items.title: How routines, rituals and rites of passage are foundations of an inclusive classroom
mix_items.summary: For many families, especially those whose children are disabled or neurodivergent, September is a daunting time. Children often find themselves in a classroom with new faces, spaces or routines.

mix_items.title: How bootmaking in Victorian England helps us think about the future of work
mix_items.summary: Put yourself in the shoes of a bootmaker in 19th-century England. Bootmaking was a sophisticated craft that involved cutting and stitching leather. It required skill, experience and time.

mix_items.title: Scientists were wrong about this strange mammal for nearly 40 years
mix_items.summary: A beautifully preserved fossil from Mongolia’s Gobi Desert has solved a mystery that puzzled paleontologists for nearly 40 years. Tamirkhan balcarceli shows that zhelestids were not early relatives of modern placental mammals, despite having teeth that seemed to suggest they were. Instead, the rabbit-like animal belonged to a separate lineage of small Cretaceous mammals.

mix_items.title: Turning to AI for health answers may signal anxiety, depression among young adults
mix_items.summary: Young adults who use generative artificial intelligence to ask health-related questions are more likely to screen positive for clinically significant anxiety and depression than those who do not use AI for health issues, according to a new study led by University of Florida researcher Yusen Zhai.

mix_items.title: Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending
mix_items.summary: How many times a day do we see messages about protecting our peace, setting boundaries and cutting toxic people out of our lives?

mix_items.title: James Webb reveals why planet formation is a race against time
mix_items.summary: JWST has revealed that young planetary systems lose their planet-building gas through a changing mix of powerful jets, molecular winds, and radiation-driven outflows. As the disks age and their gas disappears, giant planets face a shrinking window to build massive atmospheres.

mix_items.title: Where do nanoparticles go once they enter the body? Scientist helps shape new guidance
mix_items.summary: New international best practice guidance, co-written at ANSTO, sets out how to measure where nanoparticles like titanium dioxide end up in the body and how long they remain. The guidance has been shared by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), a forum and knowledge hub for data, analysis and best practices in public policy.

mix_items.title: An ancient human face emerges from pieced together Moroccan fossil remains
mix_items.summary: In the 1960s, a miner working at a mineral extraction site in Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, struck something far more valuable than any mineral in the area: a skull with distinctly humanlike features. After an initial examination, archaeologists excavated further and uncovered more remains, which they estimated to be around 40,000 years old. They identified the main skull as an African Neanderthal and named it Irhoud 1.

mix_items.title: Why higher prices can be a double-edged sword for digital services
mix_items.summary: Paying a steeper price for a subscription service can trigger a familiar impulse: You want to get your money's worth. For companies selling AI tools, cloud computing and other digital services, that can complicate a basic pricing strategy. Raising prices may keep some customers from signing up, but those who do pay may be motivated to use the service more.

mix_items.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
mix_items.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

mix_items.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
mix_items.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

mix_items.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
mix_items.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

mix_items.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
mix_items.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

mix_items.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .
